notes:
I've written the notes below, verse by verse. One caveat first: I ran out of search and fetch requests before reaching several of the sources you asked for, so there are gaps (listed at the end).

---

**v. 1**
- Paul first came to Corinth in Acts 18. He worked as a tentmaker and stayed more than a year and a half. He came as a witness, not as a philosopher or salesman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Hodge: "speech" is probably the way Paul preached and "wisdom" is what he preached. Paul came to them neither as a speech-maker nor as a philosopher. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary
- Carson, quoted on the same page: these verses give no excuse for lazy preparation or careless preaching. What Paul avoided was any method that leaves people praising the preacher instead of the Saviour. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

**v. 2**
- Paul made a deliberate choice to put the weight on Christ crucified. Guzik calls him "an ambassador, not a salesman." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Fee, quoted by Guzik: Paul didn't throw away all other knowledge. The crucified Messiah was simply his one focus and passion while he was in Corinth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/

**v. 3**
- Vincent thinks Paul's state came from his circumstances in Corinth. It may have been an illness, or, as some like Calvin believe, the threat of persecution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) take the weakness as personal and bodily (2 Cor 10:10; 12:7, 9; Gal 4:13). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_002.cfm
- Utley notes that Christ had to appear to Paul several times to encourage him (Acts 18:9-10; 23:11; 27:23). https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-2

**v. 4** *(a real difference between traditions: miracles, or the Spirit's inner work?)*
- Pulpit Commentary: "Corinthian words" was a proverb for fancy, showy speech. Paul's failure at Athens may have convinced him not to fight philosophers with their own weapons. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/2-4.htm
- Guzik: Paul isn't rejecting persuasive preaching (Acts 26 is an example). He is rejecting reliance on human skill to persuade. It is the preacher's job to preach and the Spirit's job to demonstrate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Barnes (Presbyterian): the proof was the miracles, the gift of tongues and the striking conversions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/2-4.htm
- Matthew Poole (Puritan): Grotius took this to mean miracles, but Vorstius and many others better understand it as the Holy Ghost's powerful inward persuasion of men's minds. Poole also argues that miracles never produced full assent in the Pharisees, so they don't count as "demonstration." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/2-4.htm
- Calvin: most interpreters limit this to miracles, but he takes it more broadly, as God's hand at work in every way through the apostle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-4.html
- JFB: the Spirit worked "then exhibited both outwardly by miracles, and inwardly by working on the heart, now in the latter and the more important way only". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_002.cfm
- Gill (Baptist): the demonstration came partly through Old Testament proofs, partly through signs, wonders and gifts, and through the Spirit guiding Paul's words. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-4.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): he believes prophecy, the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge are often at work from the pulpit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-4.html
- "Contending for the Faith" (Restoration Movement): Paul's preaching proved to be from God because of the miracles he performed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-4.html
- Barclay: the proof was changed lives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-4.html
- Cambridge Bible: it is doubtful the Holy Spirit is meant, and "more than doubtful" that "power" means miracles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-2.html
- Ray Ortlund (The Gospel Coalition): "demonstration" means proof that moves a hearer from plausibility to certainty. He calls that change of heart a miracle. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/power-in-preaching-decide-1-corinthians-215-part-1-of-3/
- Utley: it means the converts' changed lives, and may also relate to confirming signs that often attended Paul's preaching. https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-2

**v. 5**
- Guzik: what you draw people with is what you draw them to. Someone persuaded into the kingdom by human wisdom can be persuaded out of it the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/

**v. 6**
- Who are "the mature"? Some draw the line between saved and unsaved; others between mature and immature believers. Guzik points to Paul's use of "mature" for grown-up believers in Eph 4:13, 1 Cor 14:20 and Phil 3:15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Mark Taylor: the context (3:1-4) shows Paul means maturity versus immaturity. Others argue "mature" applies to all believers, just as Paul calls all Christians "saints" and "elect." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

**v. 7**
- The wisdom was "secret and hidden" because the link between the coming glory and the Messiah's shameful execution wasn't fully revealed until Christ and the apostles explained it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

**v. 8**
- Are "the rulers" humans or demons? Guzik says the debate goes back to Origen and Chrysostom. Morris favours human rulers, since Paul gives demons power but not ignorance. Guzik adds that demons may not have known the cross would disarm them (Col 2:15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Guzik: "Lord of glory" is among Paul's loftiest titles for Jesus and shows he regarded Jesus as God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Holman Christian Standard Bible (HCSB) note: "our acceptance was made possible by Christ's rejection." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62450/

**v. 9** *(heaven later, or the gospel now?)*
- Guzik: this is a paraphrase of Isaiah 64:4. Most people wrongly read it as heaven, but v. 10 says these things have already been revealed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Adam Clarke (Methodist) agrees: the words "belong to the present state", meaning the light and liberty the gospel gives now. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_210-16_commentary
- Wesley applies the verse to the blessings of the Messiah's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-corinthians-2.html
- Vance Havner: it means joys in heaven and also blessings available NOW. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

**v. 10**
- The Corinthians thought the gospel was "just the basics." Paul insists his message reaches the deep things of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- JFB: the Spirit explores God's depths and reveals them as far as we can take them in. They say this proves the personality and Godhead of the Holy Ghost. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_002.cfm

**v. 11**
- Hodge: only a divine person can reveal God's thoughts. The Spirit knows God's mind the way we know our own minds. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_210-16_commentary
- Precept Austin: since the Spirit thinks, he is a Person and not an "it." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_210-16_commentary
- Guzik: you can guess what your dog is thinking, but you can't know unless it tells you. In the same way, we know God's thoughts only if he reveals them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/

**v. 12** *(who is "we"?)*
- Vincent: "the spirit of the world" is the evil principle driving the unbelieving world, not Satan himself. Morris: it is human wisdom, not something satanic. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_corinthians_210-16_commentary
- Guzik: every believer has the Spirit and so can understand the basics, though not all believers are equally wise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Leake: "we" is primarily the apostles and prophets of the NT, who received revelation and wrote it down; all believers are included only secondarily. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

**v. 13**
- Two readings: "spiritual truths in spiritual words," or Clarke's "explaining spiritual things to spiritual persons." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Cambridge lists a further option: explaining spiritual things by the Spirit's inner promptings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cgt/1-corinthians-2.html
- Precept Austin reads the verse as being about the words of Scripture. It quotes Luther and Manton: no one understands Scripture unless the Holy Spirit opens it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59461/

**v. 14**
- Wesley: the natural man is every man who hath not the Spirit. These things can only be discerned by the aid of that Spirit, and by those spiritual senses, which he has not. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-corinthians-2.html
- Gill: this isn't a new believer but an unregenerate person, however cultivated. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/1-corinthians/2-14.html
- Spurgeon: no matter how good a person's temperament or upbringing, the natural man does not and cannot receive the things of the Spirit. He lacks the "ear" and "eye" of faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/2-14.html
- Poole notes great disputes about who is meant by the natural man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/2-14.htm
- Guzik: expecting the natural man to value spiritual things is like expecting a corpse to see. He adds that Christians can also slip into thinking like natural men. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Note: the Baptist, Reformed and Wesleyan voices I found all agree that the natural man can't understand without the Spirit. I didn't find a source setting out a Reformed-versus-Wesleyan disagreement on this verse.

**v. 15**
- Wesley: the spiritual man is "discerned by no man," meaning natural men, who understand neither what he is nor what he says. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-corinthians-2.html
- Guzik: this doesn't put Christians above criticism (much of this letter is criticism). The point is that no natural man is equipped to judge a spiritual one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/

**v. 16**
- Isaiah 40:13 speaks of Yahweh's mind, and Paul puts "mind of Christ" in its place. Guzik takes this as showing that Jesus is Yahweh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-2/
- Precept Austin: God has "implanted" the mind of Christ in believers, so that they see life increasingly from God's perspective. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-2-commentary

---

**What I couldn't find**
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** nothing on this chapter. The only New Advent result was Chrysostom's homily on 1 Cor 1:9.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.
- **Popular modern teaching** (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace): nothing.
- **Pentecostal and Lutheran:** no sources on this chapter. The nearest thing on v. 4 is Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel), and the only Lutheran voice is Luther quoted on v. 13.
- **Other commentaries:** I didn't read Ellicott, and saw only short extracts of the Pulpit Commentary and Gill.
